newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Day of Hate becomes Remembrance Day.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Day of Hate becomes Remembrance Day.

text.p: Cambodia's former communist rulers gathered in a suburban pagoda on Tuesday to remember the victims of the Khmer Rouge's "killing fields" regime.

The Cambodian People's Party (CPP) had in the past marked May 20 as a "Day of Hate" against the Maoist group, but after a year of momentous change within the Khmer Rouge it changed the name this year to "Remembrance Day."

Thousands of Khmer Rouge guerrillas have defected to the government since former top guerrilla official Ieng Sary split last August with hardliners loyal to Pol Pot, leader of the 1975-79 regime blamed for the deaths of more than one million people through execution, disease and overwork.

"We have stopped using the words 'Day of Hate' because we don't want people to say the Cambodian People's Party still harbours hatred and anger, so we chose the words 'Remembrance Day'," a CPP official told Reuters.

The three top CPP leaders, party chief Chea Sim, co-Premier Hun Sen and Heng Samrin, led some 6,000 people in mourning the dead at a ceremony in a pagoda in Phnom Penh's Takhmau suburb, regarded as a stronghold of the former communist party.

All three men once fought alongside the Khmer Rouge before fleeing to Vietnam in the late 1970s. They were made leaders of the communist Kampuchean People's Revolutionary Party regime installed after Vietnamese forces invaded Cambodia and ousted the Khmer Rouge in 1979.
The party later changed its name and embraced multi-party democracy and a market economy before a 1991 peace accord with rivals, including the Khmer Rouge.
It formed an uneasy coalition with the royalist FUNCINPEC government after U.N.-run elections in 1993 but the relationship between the two parties has deteriorated to a new low in recent weeks.
The royalists have ignored the Day of Hate, saying it runs counter to the spirit of reconciliation.
Rival premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen successfully lobbied for a royal pardon for Ieng Sary, sentenced to death in absentia in 1979 for his role in the killings of the 1970s.
The two premiers have since been vying to win the allegiance of the thousands of guerrillas who followed Ieng Sary's example by defecting.
